summary: Defines algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for DNSSEC, to make sure there is at least one algorithm that all implementations support. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 9904.

plainLanguage.summary: DNSSEC uses digital signatures, and digital signatures need an algorithm. This RFC says which algorithms every implementation must handle, which it may still use but should avoid, and which must no longer be used at all, so that all DNSSEC software keeps working together.

what is the recommended dnssec algorithm
subtitle: Which signing and digest algorithms DNSSEC software must, should or must not support.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC signs DNS data with cryptographic algorithms, and resolvers and authoritative servers have to agree on at least one algorithm they both support or signed zones fail to validate.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists every DNSSEC algorithm with a requirement level for signing and a separate level for validation, using the RFC 2119 words. It requires ECDSAP256SHA256 and RSASHA256 for both, treats SHA-1 as mandatory to validate but not to sign, and recommends SHA-256 for delegation records.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8624 was a Proposed Standard. It has been obsoleted by RFC 9904 and updated by RFC 9157.

sections.title: Why the List Is Rewritten Periodically
sections.content:
DNSSEC uses various cryptographic algorithms to provide authentication of DNS data and proof of nonexistence. To ensure interoperability between DNS resolvers and DNS authoritative servers, it is necessary to specify a set of algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidelines that ensures at least one algorithm that all implementations support. This document defines the current algorithm implementation requirements and usage guidance for DNSSEC, and obsoletes RFC 6944.

The reason for periodic revision is stated plainly. The field of cryptography evolves continuously. New, stronger algorithms appear, and existing algorithms are found to be less secure than originally thought. Attacks previously thought to be computationally infeasible become more accessible as the available computational resources increase. The choices for algorithms must be conservative to minimise the risk of algorithm compromise.

The document only speaks about algorithms it names. Any algorithm listed in the DNSKEY and DS registries that is not mentioned in this document may be implemented. An algorithm is specified as MAY in this document only when it has been downgraded from a MUST or a RECOMMENDED to a MAY.
sections.plainLanguage: Crypto changes over time: algorithms get weaker as computing power grows, so the list of acceptable algorithms has to be reissued every so often.

sections.title: How Algorithms Are Deprecated and Introduced
sections.content:
The mandatory-to-implement algorithm of tomorrow should already be available in most implementations of DNSSEC by the time it is made mandatory. The document tries to identify and introduce those algorithms in advance, while noting that there is no guarantee that the algorithms in use today will become mandatory in the future, and that published algorithms are continuously subjected to cryptographic attack and may become too weak or even be completely broken before the document is updated.

Deprecation is expected to be gradual, in a series of updates, which gives implementations time to update while remaining interoperable. Unless there are strong security reasons, an algorithm is expected to be downgraded from MUST to NOT RECOMMENDED or MAY, rather than straight to MUST NOT. An algorithm that has not been mentioned as mandatory-to-implement is expected to be introduced with a RECOMMENDED instead of a MUST.

There is a practical consequence for zone operators. Because the effect of using an unknown DNSKEY algorithm is that the zone is treated as insecure, it is recommended that algorithms downgraded to NOT RECOMMENDED or lower not be used by authoritative nameservers and DNSSEC signers to create new DNSKEYs. That allows deprecated algorithms to become less and less common over time. Once an algorithm has reached a sufficiently low level of deployment it can be marked MUST NOT, so that recursive resolvers can remove support for validating it. Recursive nameservers are encouraged to retain support for all algorithms not marked MUST NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: Nothing is switched off overnight. An algorithm is first discouraged, then quietly dropped, and only once almost nobody uses it is it removed from the must-validate list.

sections.title: The DNSKEY Algorithm Table
sections.content:
The table gives, for each DNSKEY algorithm, one requirement level for signing and a separate level for validation. Signing means creating signatures; validation means checking them.

The document then explains the entries. RSAMD5 is not widely deployed, and there is an industry-wide trend to deprecate MD5 usage. RSASHA1 and RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 are widely deployed, although the zones deploying them are recommended to switch to ECDSAP256SHA256, because there is an industry-wide trend to move to elliptic curve cryptography. RSASHA1 does not support NSEC3, while RSASHA1-NSEC3-SHA1 can be used with or without it. DSA and DSA-NSEC3-SHA1 are not widely deployed and are vulnerable to private key compromise when generating signatures using a weak or compromised random number generator.

RSASHA256 is widely used and considered strong. It has been the default algorithm for a number of years and is now slowly being replaced with ECDSAP256SHA256 because of the latter's shorter key and signature size, which results in smaller DNS packets. RSASHA512 is not recommended for DNSSEC signing because it has not seen wide deployment, but some deployments exist, so DNSSEC validation must implement it to ensure interoperability. There is no significant difference in cryptographic strength between RSASHA512 and RSASHA256, and its use is discouraged because it will only make the deprecation of older algorithms harder.

ECC-GOST, which is GOST R 34.10-2001, has been superseded by GOST R 34.10-2012, and that later version has not been standardized for use in DNSSEC.

ECDSAP256SHA256 provides more cryptographic strength with a shorter signature length than either RSASHA256 or RSASHA512. It has been widely deployed, so it is now at MUST level for both validation and signing. It is recommended to use the deterministic digital signature generation procedure of ECDSA, specified in RFC 6979, when implementing ECDSAP256SHA256 and ECDSAP384SHA384. ECDSAP384SHA384 shares the same properties but offers a modest security advantage of 192 bits of strength against 128 bits. For most DNSSEC applications ECDSAP256SHA256 should be satisfactory and robust for the foreseeable future and is therefore recommended for signing, while a DNSSEC use case requiring 192-bit security strength is unlikely to arise.

ED25519 and ED448 use the Edwards-curve Digital Security Algorithm. The document lists three main advantages of EdDSA: it does not require the use of a unique random number for each signature, there are no padding or truncation issues as with ECDSA, and it is more resilient to side-channel attacks. EdDSA is also less prone to implementation errors. It is expected that ED25519 will become the future recommended default algorithm once there is enough support in deployed DNSSEC validators.
sections.plainLanguage: Each algorithm gets two grades: one for creating signatures and one for checking them. Signing is stricter than validating, because a validator that drops an algorithm stops validating old zones, while a signer that drops one just stops producing old-style signatures.

sections.title: The DS and CDS Algorithm Table
sections.content:
The second table covers Delegation Signer digest algorithms, and the same recommendations apply to the Child Delegation Signer record type specified in RFC 7344. The NULL entry is a special case: it is a CDS record that signals removal of the DS record at the parent, as described in RFC 8078.

SHA-1 is still widely used for Delegation Signer records, so validators must implement its validation, but it must not be used to generate new DS and CDS records. SHA-256 is widely used and considered strong. GOST R 34.11-94 has been superseded by GOST R 34.11-2012, which has not been standardized for use in DNSSEC. SHA-384 shares the same properties as SHA-256 but offers a modest security advantage of 384 bits of strength against 256 bits; for most applications SHA-256 should be satisfactory and robust for the foreseeable future and is therefore recommended for DS and CDS records, while a use case requiring 384-bit strength is unlikely to arise.

The operational recommendation for new and existing deployments is stated separately: SHA-256 is the recommended DS and CDS algorithm.
sections.plainLanguage: DS records are the small pointers that link a parent zone to a child's signature key. They use a hash, and the hash is chosen differently from the one used for signing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security of cryptographic systems depends on the strength of the algorithms chosen and the strength of the keys used with them, and also on the engineering of the protocol so that there are no non-cryptographic ways to bypass the security of the overall system.

The algorithms this document marks as MUST or RECOMMENDED to implement are not known to be broken, in the cryptographic sense, at the current time, and research so far suggests they are likely to remain secure into the foreseeable future. That is not a permanent guarantee, and new revisions of the document are expected from time to time to reflect current best practice.

The document then gives the reason for the slow deprecation policy. Retiring an algorithm too soon would result in a zone signed with a retired algorithm being downgraded to the equivalent of an unsigned zone. Algorithm deprecation must therefore be done very slowly, and only after careful consideration and measurement of its use.
sections.plainLanguage: Pulling an algorithm out of use too early would make every zone still signed with it look unsigned, so the process has to be slow and evidence-driven.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
DNSKEY algorithm rollover in a live zone is a complex process, and the RFC points to RFC 6781 and RFC 7583 for guidelines on how to perform algorithm rollovers. DS algorithm rollover in a live zone is also a complex process.

One rule is stated as a MUST. Upgrading an algorithm at the same time as rolling a new Key Signing Key will lead to DNSSEC validation failures. Administrators must complete the process of the DS algorithm upgrade before starting a rollover process for a new KSK.
sections.plainLanguage: Change the hash and the signing key at the same time and validation will break. Do them one after the other.
